content:
{'translation': "In scorching hot weather, whether bus compartments will turn into 'hot ovens' affecting the health of bus captains and passengers has raised public concern. Kowloon Motor Bus (KMB), which had originally 'locked' the compartment air conditioning at 25 degrees, recently stated that it would gradually lower the compartment air conditioning to 24 degrees Celsius and maximum airflow; Citybus stated that the air conditioning is generally set at 23.5 degrees Celsius. 'Our China Journalism Hub' (集誌社) today (the 13th) conducted real-time temperature measurements on buses across multiple routes at different time periods. Among them, on a KMB route running from Fanling to Wan Chai during noon, the temperatures on the upper and lower decks of the compartment remained at around 32 degrees Celsius. When passing through the section at the Tai Lam Tunnel, the air vents suddenly blew out hot air at 40 degrees Celsius. Many passengers on the bus were sweating from their chests, and one passenger holding a portable fan described it, saying, 'This is the first time I've used a fan on a bus, it feels so stuffy, I feel like I can't breathe.'", 'index': 0}

{'translation': 'The scorching hot weather eased slightly today, with temperatures in the northern district approaching 33.6°C at noon. A bus at the Wah Ming Estate terminus in Fanling, under the blazing sun, had a body surface temperature as high as 38.7°C.', 'index': 1}

{'translation': 'Buses from the northern district to Hong Kong Island reached a maximum of 33.7°C inside the compartments', 'index': 2}

{'translation': "There were localised showers today, and the scorching hot weather eased slightly. At noon, temperatures in the northern district approached 33.6°C. Our reporter took KMB Route 978 from Fanling, departing from the Wah Ming Estate terminus and heading to the Wan Chai Convention and Exhibition Centre terminus. Before departure, the bus was exposed to harsh sunlight, and a handheld infrared thermometer measured the bus body surface temperature at 38.7°C. After boarding, the instrument panel above the driver's seat showed that the bus air conditioning was set at 25 degrees and had not yet been lowered. The compartment was like an oven, and after the bus departed, the compartment temperature reached 33.7°C, then remained fluctuating between 32°C and 33°C.", 'index': 3}

{'translation': 'The bus arrived at Sheung Shui town centre after about 15 minutes of travel. After the air conditioning had been running for some time, the compartment temperature gradually dropped to 28°C. After travelling for nearly 20 minutes, with little shade along the way, when the bus reached the section before the Tai Lam Tunnel in Yuen Long, the ventilation vents at the front and rear of the upper deck suddenly blew out a burst of hot air, with the thermometer showing as high as 40°C. Under waves of hot air, the upper deck was noticeably more stuffy. The temperature at the front and rear of the compartment rose to nearly 32°C, the middle section was about 30°C, while the lower deck remained at around 28.6°C.', 'index': 4}

{'translation': 'After travelling for about 35 minutes to the section before the Tai Lam Tunnel, hot air at 40°C suddenly blasted out from the front and rear positions of the upper deck. The compartment was stuffy, and the temperature rose to nearly 32°C.', 'index': 5}

{'translation': "40°C hot air blasting out — Passenger: It feels so stuffy, I feel like I can't breathe", 'index': 6}

{'translation': "Among the citizens who sat in the seats under the ventilation vents throughout the journey, some had sweat breaking out on their chests, while others took out small fans to cool down. Among them, Mr. Yung, who was wearing a vest, was sweating from his chest. He said he could clearly feel the hot air blowing from the ventilation vents, and pointed out that the entire bus compartment was equally 'stuffy' and poorly ventilated.", 'index': 7}

{'translation': 'Mr. Yung, who was sitting under the ventilation vent, was sweating even though he was wearing a vest, saying that the compartment was very stuffy.', 'index': 8}

{'translation': "A female passenger pointed out that the temperature was still acceptable when the bus first departed, but hot air blew out when the bus reached the midway point, forcing her to use a mini fan on the bus for the first time, saying, 'It feels so stuffy, I feel like I can't breathe.' She said that compared to her previous rides, the temperature inside the compartment was noticeably higher this time. She also noted that she was aware KMB would lower the compartment air conditioning to 24°C, but believed the ideal temperature should be 22 to 23°C, hoping that KMB could flexibly adjust the compartment temperature according to the requirements of different routes and weather conditions.", 'index': 9}

{'translation': "Ms. Chu, who is in her seventies, initially said that the compartment temperature was still acceptable and that she did not need to use the fan hanging in front of her chest. However, during the bus journey, she decided to turn on the fan, saying, 'It's a bit hot, I've broken out in some sweat.' Ms. Chu said she relies on KMB for her daily commute, usually taking routes within the northern district, and that Route 978 was even hotter than other routes. She also said that if the compartment temperature did not improve, she would consider taking other modes of transport.", 'index': 10}

{'translation': "The compartment temperature rose to 31.7°C. Some passengers had to turn on their fans to cool down, while others said, 'It feels so stuffy, I feel like I can't breathe.'", 'index': 11}

{'translation': 'Unions voice concern over impact on driving safety — KMB gradually lowers air conditioning to 24°C', 'index': 12}

{'translation': "The KMB Staff Rights Union recently pointed out that the bus compartment air conditioning is set by the company at 25°C, which is too high with insufficient airflow, directly affecting the occupational health and driving safety of bus captains. They have arranged a meeting with the Labour Relations Division and requested the Labour Department to intervene. The Motor Transport Workers General Union also pointed out that KMB's compartment air conditioning temperature is 'locked' at 25°C, and the airflow system has been 'pressed down to a feeble state', making the compartments extremely stuffy, leaving bus captains with no choice but to 'suffer in silence'.", 'index': 13}

{'translation': "KMB subsequently stated that it has begun lowering the compartment air conditioning to 24°C and maximum airflow. The KMB Staff Rights Union stressed that lowering the temperature is only the first step; the company must ensure that the air conditioning systems of all vehicles are functioning properly, with sufficient airflow, and continuously monitor actual compartment temperatures, so that 'the measures will not remain mere statements of principle'.", 'index': 14}

{'translation': "When responding to enquiries yesterday, KMB did not provide specific responses regarding how many buses have completed the temperature adjustment and how many have yet to be done. It reiterated that, in response to the persistently and abnormally scorching hot weather in recent days, with record-breaking high temperatures recorded, it has begun lowering the compartment temperature settings. It noted that 'it will take time to fully complete the relevant work' and that it will do so as soon as possible. It also stated that it will continue to inspect all compartment air conditioning systems and monitor compartment temperatures.", 'index': 15}

{'translation': "Citybus stated yesterday (the 12th) that its fleet's air conditioning systems are equipped with thermostatic devices, generally set at 23.5°C. This setting takes into account factors such as the need for buses to stop frequently and open doors for passenger boarding and alighting during operations, resulting in the loss of cool air inside the compartment, to ensure that the compartment temperature can be maintained at a stable and comfortable level. The company will step up monitoring of compartment temperatures in response to the scorching hot weather.", 'index': 16}
